stem: A 52-year-old man is scheduled for elective surgery. He is a chronic smoker with well-controlled hypertension and no end-organ damage. His vital signs are stable, and physical examination is unremarkable. What is his American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification?
expl: ASA II = mild systemic disease without functional limitation. Well-controlled hypertension and smoking without end-organ damage fit ASA II (the slide table lists "cigarette smoking without COPD" under ASA 2).

why.A: ASA I is a healthy non-smoker with no disease.
why.B: ASA IV = severe disease that is a constant threat to life.
why.C: ASA III = severe disease with functional limitation (e.g. poorly controlled HTN, morbid obesity).
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 70-year-old female with atrial fibrillation on chronic warfarin therapy is scheduled for elective surgery. Her INR is 2.8. What is the most appropriate preoperative management?

opts.t: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and consider bridging with LMWH.
Stop warfarin 1 day before surgery without bridging.
Continue warfarin and closely monitor INR.
Give the patient Vitamin K before the surgery

expl: AF on warfarin before elective surgery: stop warfarin ~5 days before so the INR normalizes, and bridge with LMWH when thrombotic risk is high.

why.A: Correct — 5 days lets the INR fall to normal; LMWH covers the thrombotic risk meanwhile.
why.B: One day is far too short; warfarin's effect lasts several days, so the INR would still be high.
why.C: Operating at INR 2.8 means a high bleeding risk for an elective case.
why.D: Vitamin K is for urgent reversal; in elective surgery you simply stop warfarin in time.

stem: Which of the following patients requires an extensive preoperative assessment?

opts.t: A 24 year old healthy male undergoing an elective surgery
A 30 year old healthy female undergoing a skin excision under local anesthesia
A 40 year old female with controlled hypertension undergoing an elective surgery
A 60 year old male with atrial fibrillation and uncontrolled congestive heart failure

expl: The extent of pre-op assessment depends on comorbidity. Uncontrolled CHF with AF is a high-risk patient who needs full work-up and optimization.

why.A: Healthy young patient — minimal or no testing.
why.B: Healthy patient, minor procedure under local — minimal assessment.
why.C: Controlled hypertension = mild systemic disease (ASA II); routine assessment is enough.
why.D: Correct — uncontrolled heart failure + arrhythmia: high perioperative cardiac risk needing extensive assessment and optimization.

stem: A smoker, otherwise healthy man is undergoing an elective surgery, which of the following would be best to prevent postop pulmonary complications?

opts.t: Routine preoperative pulmonary function testing for all smokers

expl: Stopping smoking 4–6 weeks before surgery lets ciliary function and sputum clear, lowering post-op pulmonary complications (the doctor gave ~6 weeks).

why.A: Correct — the only option that removes the cause in time.
why.B: Treats bronchospasm after the fact; doesn't prevent complications.
why.C: Spirometry exercises help, but stopping smoking has the biggest effect.
why.D: Routine PFTs for all smokers are not indicated and don't prevent anything.

stem: A patient with a family history of malignant hyperthermia is undergoing elective surgery. What can you do to prevent it?

opts.t: Avoid depolarizing muscle relaxants and volatile agents
Avoid volatile and just use depolarizing muscle relaxants
Use depolarizing but make sure dantrolene is available in OR

expl: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine (a depolarizing relaxant). Prevention = avoid both (use TIVA); dantrolene is the treatment.

why.C: Dantrolene availability does not make a trigger safe; you still avoid it.
why.D: No need to postpone — just use a trigger-free anesthetic.

stem: A 60-year-old man underwent PCI with a drug-eluting stent (DES) three months ago. He is currently on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) and is scheduled for elective non-cardiac surgery next month. What is the recommended timing for elective surgery after DES placement?

opts.t: Proceed with surgery now after stopping dual antiplatelet therapy 6 days before surgery

expl: After a drug-eluting stent, elective non-cardiac surgery is delayed until dual antiplatelet therapy can safely stop — at least about 6 months — because stopping DAPT early risks stent thrombosis.

why.A: Too early — high stent thrombosis risk.
why.B: One month is the minimum for a bare-metal stent, not a DES.
why.D: Stopping DAPT 3 months after a DES is dangerous (stent thrombosis → MI).

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of DVT is scheduled for elective surgery. He is on warfarin and has been bridged with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) preoperatively. How long should LMWH be stopped before surgery to minimize bleeding risk?
expl: Therapeutic-dose LMWH is stopped 24 hours before surgery (prophylactic dose ~12 h) to limit bleeding.

why.A: 10 hours is not enough for a therapeutic dose.
why.B: 12 hours applies to prophylactic doses, not "all patients".
why.D: Continuing until surgery causes major bleeding.

stem: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. His baseline oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Which of the following is the most effective strategy to prevent postoperative respiratory failure?

opts.t: Effective pain management and incentive spirometry

expl: In severe COPD, post-op respiratory failure comes from shallow breathing because of pain and atelectasis. Good analgesia + incentive spirometry keeps the lungs expanded.

why.A: Pre-op rehab helps but is not the most effective single measure in this setting.
why.C: Oxygen alone doesn't prevent atelectasis or sputum retention.
why.D: Chest physiotherapy alone, without pain control, is less effective.

stem: A 60-year-old man has been taking prednisolone 15 mg daily for chronic autoimmune disease. He is scheduled for thoracic surgery. What is the most appropriate management of his steroid therapy on the day of surgery?

opts.t: Take usual morning steroid dose; just before induction, give IV hydrocortisone 50 mg, then 25 mg IV every 8 hours
Take usual morning steroid dose; just before induction, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, then 50 mg IV every 8 hours × 6 doses
Take usual morning steroid dose only

expl: Chronic steroids (≥5 mg prednisolone for >3 weeks) suppress the HPA axis. Thoracic surgery is MAJOR surgery → usual morning dose + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg q8h.

why.C: Not enough cover for major surgery → risk of adrenal crisis.
why.D: Stopping steroids can cause an Addisonian crisis.

stem: A 70-year-old man is scheduled for bilateral knee replacement. During the preoperative verification, the surgical team notes the wrong knee is listed for surgery. The patient confirms it is the opposite knee, and the surgical site has not been marked yet. What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Perform a preoperative “time-out” and verification with the surgical team and patient before marking the correct site
Proceed and check later in the operating room
Cancel the surgery and reschedule without further verification

expl: Wrong-site surgery is prevented by verification with the patient and team (time-out) and correct site marking before surgery.

why.B: Leaving verification to the OR invites a wrong-site error.
why.C: Cancelling is unnecessary; the error can be corrected by verification.
why.D: Site decisions are never left to intra-operative judgement.

stem: A patient admitted for elective surgery suddenly develops shock and becomes confused, requiring emergency surgical intervention. There is no available family member or contact to provide consent. What is the most appropriate course of action?

opts.t: Continue trying to find a family member
Perform the surgery immediately because it is an emergency
Delay surgery until consent is obtained

expl: Life-threatening emergency, patient lacks capacity, no surrogate available → implied consent; operate immediately.

why.A: Cancelling would let the patient die.
why.B: Searching for family delays life-saving surgery.
why.D: Waiting for consent in shock is unsafe.

stem: A 30-years-old female with Myasthenia Gravis on 10mg of Prednisolone. Going to have an inguinal hernia repair. What should be changed on her medications regimen before the surgery?

opts.t: Continue and give Hydrocortisone 100 mg on anesthesia induction
Continue and give Hydrocortisone 50 mg on anesthesia induction

expl: Inguinal hernia repair is MINOR surgery. Patients on chronic steroids take their usual dose; no extra hydrocortisone is needed for minor procedures.

why.A: Stopping steroids risks adrenal crisis and myasthenic worsening.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 62-year-old male found to have an incidental gallbladder polyp of 1.2cm, he had PCI 5 weeks ago with drug eluting stent, he is on Aspirin and Clopidogrel. Which of the following is true regarding surgery?

opts.t: Send to the OR after 7 days
Do laparoscopy after a year and stop clopidogrel 7 days prior to the surgery
He can’t do surgery at anytime because of high cardiac risk

expl: DES placed 5 weeks ago and an incidental, non-urgent gallbladder polyp → wait until DAPT can be stopped (older guidance 1 year), then stop clopidogrel ~7 days before laparoscopy.

why.A: Operating now on DAPT, 5 weeks after a DES, is high risk and not needed.
why.B: Stopping clopidogrel 5 weeks after a DES risks stent thrombosis.
why.D: He can have surgery — just later.

stem: What is the recommended time for NPO ?
expl: Standard fasting is 6–8 hours for solids (clear fluids up to 2 hours).

why.C: 4 hours is breast milk in infants.
why.D: 6 hours alone is the minimum for a light meal/formula; the standard answer is 6–8 h.

stem: What is the recommended time to stop smoking prior to surgery?
expl: Smoking cessation 4–6 weeks before surgery improves ciliary function and lowers pulmonary and wound complications.

why.D: Longer is fine but 4–6 weeks is the recommended answer.

stem: What is the best time to stop Warfarin before surgery?
expl: Warfarin is stopped 5 days before surgery so the INR normalizes.

why.A: Day of surgery is too late.
why.B: 2 days is too short for warfarin.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A smoker is scheduled for elective surgery. When should they stop smoking to minimize postoperative complications?
expl: 4–6 weeks of cessation reduces post-op pulmonary complications.

stem: Patient comes to the anesthesia clinic for preoperative assessment and she is discussing with the doctor the medications that she should stop and the medication that she can continue using before the operation. Which one of the following (medications)s she can continue using?
expl: Beta-blockers and statins are continued peri-operatively (stopping them causes rebound tachycardia/ischemia). ACEI/ARB are usually held on the morning of surgery (hypotension under anesthesia); warfarin is stopped.

why.C: Usually held the morning of surgery.
why.D: Usually held the morning of surgery.

stem: Which patient requires ECG preoperatively?

opts.t: 60 years male for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
22 years female for elective breast implants

expl: A pre-op ECG is indicated by age (older patients) or cardiac risk factors — the 60-year-old.

why.B: Young healthy patient — no ECG needed.
why.C: Young healthy patient — no ECG needed.
why.D: "Adult" alone is not an indication.

stem: a long emergency case what should you do regarding the surgery consent?

opts.t: Hold OR and wait for spouse consent
2 surgeons call the spouse and sign in behalf of her
No need for consent because it’s an emergency

expl: In a true emergency where the patient can't consent and no one is available, implied consent applies.

why.A: Holding a life-saving operation is wrong.
why.C: A fingerprint from an incapacitated patient is not valid consent.
why.D: Correct (source key).

stem: in pregnant lady, which trimester is the safest to operate surgically?
expl: The second trimester is the safest time for non-obstetric surgery: organogenesis is complete (less teratogenic/miscarriage risk than the 1st) and the uterus is not yet large enough to cause preterm labour or obstruct the field (3rd).

why.A: Not all months are equally safe.
why.C: Risk of preterm labour; the uterus limits access.
why.D: Organogenesis — highest miscarriage/teratogenic risk.

stem: A 20 year old male is completely healthy. will undergo inguinal hernia repair surgery. what is the pre-operative assessment needed for him?
expl: A healthy 20-year-old (ASA I) for minor surgery needs no routine investigations.

why.D: Not indicated.

stem: A case about a patient who has done a successful non-complicated laparoscopic appendectomy, and asked about how to prevent surgical infections in this patient ?

opts.t: Pre-op cefazolin, during the surgery, and for 72 hours post-op

expl: For uncomplicated appendicitis/appendectomy, a peri-operative dose of a cephalosporin + metronidazole (covers gut aerobes and anaerobes) is enough; no prolonged post-op course.

why.A: Cefazolin lacks anaerobic cover and 72 hours post-op is unnecessary.

stem: female known case of systemic lupus erythematosus and is taking prednisone for her condition 2 months ago for 3 days. She is scheduled to have a inguinal hernia .What should be done regarding her steroids?

opts.t: Double the dose of prednisone the day prior to the surgery
50 mg hydrocortisone IV just before the procedure and 25 mg of hydrocortisone every 8 hr for 24hr.
Double the dose the day after the surgery

expl: A 3-day course 2 months ago does not suppress the HPA axis → no stress-dose steroids needed.

why.C: That's the regimen for a patient currently on steroids having moderate surgery.
why.D: Not needed.

stem: A patient presented with a life-threatening vascular injury after a RTA. No watcher was there in the scene. What to do regarding his consent?

opts.t: Try to find a family member
Try to get a verbal consent from a family member

expl: Life-threatening injury and no one available → implied consent; treat immediately.

why.D: Not required in an emergency.

stem: Patient undergoing elective lap chole, he has hypothyroidism. What should you do?

opts.t: Give levothyroxine on the day of operation.
Reschedule operation until the patient is euthyroid.

expl: Uncorrected hypothyroidism → myxedema coma, hypotension, slow recovery. Elective surgery is postponed until euthyroid.

why.A: Unnecessary risk for an elective case.
why.B: One dose on the day of surgery won't correct hypothyroidism.
why.D: Correct.

stem: 20 year old known to have reactive respiratory disease, scheduled for a laparoscopic hernia repair, in holding area developed severe wheezing. What is the best way to manage this patient?

opts.t: Administer spinal anesthesia with intravenous steroids.
Administer local anesthesia with sedation and avoid unnecessary airway manipulation.
Administer nebulizer and procedure with surgery.

expl: Acute severe bronchospasm before an elective operation → postpone and optimize; operating risks peri-op respiratory failure.

why.A: Not appropriate for an elective case in active bronchospasm.
why.B: Still exposes an unstable airway to risk; elective surgery can wait.
why.C: Proceeding the same day is unsafe.
why.D: Correct.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding why obese pt are at an increased risk of complications during surgery

opts.t: Procedures could take a longer time

expl: Obese patients are at higher risk partly because procedures take longer (and are technically harder), plus airway, wound and VTE problems.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding Thyroid surgeries

opts.t: There’s a possibility of developing Myxedema coma post surgery in Hypothyroid pt

expl: Hypothyroid patients may develop myxedema coma after surgery — another reason to make them euthyroid before elective surgery.

stem: Tight control of sugar level in a diabetic patient undergoing surgery:

opts.t: Decrease the incidence of deep wound infection

expl: Tight peri-operative glucose control lowers surgical-site (deep wound) infection.

why.B: Not a benefit of glucose control.
why.C: Phagocytosis improves, but the tested outcome is fewer infections.
why.D: Wrong — glucose control clearly improves outcomes.

stem: A 65 y/o male is planned to have a right hemicolectomy for colon cancer. Which of the following would have a beneficial effect on his metabolic response to surgery?

opts.t: Performing the surgery using a laparoscopic approach.
keeping the patient fasting for 3 days after surgery.

expl: The metabolic (stress) response is proportional to tissue injury. Laparoscopy reduces the trauma and therefore the catabolic/inflammatory response (an ERAS principle).

why.A: Paracetamol is analgesia; it doesn't modify the metabolic response meaningfully.
why.D: Prolonged fasting worsens catabolism; early feeding is recommended.

stem: patient came to the hospital for open hernia repair as day surgery. Which of the following services do you need to assess the patient preoperatively?
expl: Every day-surgery patient is assessed by anesthesia beforehand (fitness for anesthesia and same-day discharge).

why.A: Only if a blood disorder exists.
why.D: Only if lung disease exists.

stem: A 55-year-old male is planned for hernia repair. He is comprehensive with no mental illness. During the preoperative assessment visit, he didn't come to the clinic and his 20-year-old son came to sign the consent on his behalf. What is the most appropriate action?

opts.t: Ask for the older brother to sign the consent
Ask for the patient himself to sign the consent
Get the medical director approval for the son to sign the consent
Let the son sign the consent

expl: A competent adult must sign his own consent; relatives can't consent for a patient who has capacity.

why.C: Not needed — the patient can sign.
why.D: The son can't consent for a competent father.

stem: 25 female known case of systemic lupus erythematosus and is taking prednisone for her condition. She is scheduled to have a total knee replacement.What should be done regarding her steroids?

opts.t: Double the dose of prednisone the day prior to the surgery
50 mg hydrocortisone IV just before the procedure and 25 mg of hydrocortisone every 8 hr for 24hr.
Double the dose the day after the surgery

expl: Patient currently on steroids + total knee replacement (MODERATE surgery) → hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction, then 25 mg q8h for 24 h.

why.A: She is on steroids now, so supplementation is needed.
why.B: Doubling oral prednisone the day before is not the regimen.
why.D: Not the regimen.

stem: 29 years old female presented with epigastric pain and vomiting underwent endoscopy to rule out cholecystitis. No cholecystitis but a 5 cm splenic artery aneurysm was found. She is symptomatic and planning to get pregnant and there was no interventional radiologist in the hospital so the doctor decided to do elective splenectomy. When is the best timing to give vaccines prior to the operation to prevent infection by encapsulated bacteria ?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: For elective splenectomy, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae b) at least 2 weeks (2–3 weeks) before surgery so that the immune response develops while the spleen is still present. In emergency splenectomy, vaccinate ~14 days after.

why.B: The policy for emergency cases, not elective.
why.C: Too late for an antibody response.
why.D: Used only when the splenectomy was unplanned.

stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease. What to do preoperatively to reduce his bleeding risk?
expl: Uremic bleeding is due to platelet dysfunction; desmopressin (DDAVP) releases vWF/factor VIII and improves platelet function.

why.B: Vitamin K corrects clotting factors, not uremic platelets.
why.C: FFP replaces factors; not the problem here.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A smoker patient undergoing lung surgery. When should he stop smoking before the surgery to reduce the risk for post-operative lung problems?
expl: Stop smoking at least ~6 weeks before lung surgery (the doctor's example was ~6 weeks).

why.B: Longer than needed for the standard answer.
why.D: 4 weeks is the minimum; for lung surgery the keyed answer is 6 weeks.

stem: A patient scheduled for abdominal aortic aneurysm repair with synthetic graft. He is allergic to penicillin. Which antibiotic prophylaxis should you give the patient ?
expl: Prosthetic graft surgery needs anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis. With penicillin allergy, use clindamycin (or vancomycin) instead of cefazolin.

why.A: Cefazolin is avoided in significant penicillin allergy; metronidazole isn't needed.
why.D: Cefepime is a broad treatment agent, not prophylaxis.

stem: Which trimester is safe for surgery in pregnant women ?
expl: The second trimester is safest: organogenesis is complete (less teratogenic risk than the 1st) and preterm labour is less likely than in the 3rd.

why.C: Higher risk of preterm labour and technical difficulty.
why.D: The risks are not the same.

stem: Scenario then question : when to withhold rapid acting insulin ?
expl: When NPO from midnight, rapid-acting (prandial) insulin is held from midnight because there is no meal to cover; basal insulin is usually continued at a reduced dose.

why.B: Continuing prandial insulin while fasting → hypoglycemia.
why.D: Holding only at the time of surgery is too late.

stem: What is done in “sign in” ?

opts.t: marking the site of the patient

srcNote: Both A and B are correct (Pre-operative assessment)
expl: The WHO "sign in" (before induction) confirms the patient's identity, the site, procedure and consent, and checks that the site is marked. The source listed both A and B as correct; confirming identity (B) is the core step — the marking itself is done earlier and only checked here. "Anticipating critical events" and team introductions belong to the time-out.

why.A: Accepted by the source too — sign-in checks that the site has been marked.
why.B: Correct — confirming identity is the core of sign-in.
why.D: Belongs to the time-out.

stem: A60-year-old male is planned for colon resection. He is known to have liver Cirrhosis. He is class A (child-pugh classification), What is the anticipated mortality rate?
expl: Surgical mortality by Child-Pugh class: A ≈ 10%, B ≈ 30%, C ≈ 76–82%.

why.D: Not a Child-Pugh value.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on warfarin is scheduled to have elective hernia repair. What is your advice for the patient regarding the warfarin use?

opts.t: Warfarin dose should continue the same
It should be stopped 2 days before OR
It should be stopped 1 week before the surgery
It should be continued in lower doses

expl: Warfarin is stopped before elective surgery (≈5 days; this older key says 1 week).

why.D: Lowering the dose still leaves the patient anticoagulated.

stem: a Patient with child -Pugh class (a) cirrhosis with sigmoid cancer what’s the mortality rate if surgery is performed for him?
expl: Child-Pugh class predicts operative mortality: A ≈ 10% (<10%), B ≈ 30%, C ≈ 75–80%.

why.D: Class B (~30%).

stem: A Lady who will undergo elective plastic surgery , which of the following history information will affect the surgical results?
expl: Smoking (nicotine vasoconstriction, carbon monoxide) impairs skin/flap perfusion and wound healing — it directly worsens plastic-surgery results. An IUD has no effect.

stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis is at the clinic for (operative assessment). The surgeon asks you to calculate the Child-Pugh score. What element is needed to calculate the score?
srcNote: (Pre-Operative Assessment) In child-pugh score we use: albumin, total bilirubin, INR (or PT), ascites, hepatic encephalopathy.
expl: Child-Pugh = bilirubin (total), albumin, INR/PT, ascites, encephalopathy.

why.D: Total, not indirect, bilirubin.

stem: Patient with atrial fibrillation booked for lumpectomy in breast. She is taking warfarin. What would you tell her regarding warfarin?
srcNote: (Pre-Operative Assessment) From 3 to 5 days preoperatively and IV heparin should be started; heparin should be discontinued from 4 to 6 hours preoperatively and can be restarted postoperatively; then warfarin can be restarted in a few days. Source note (435 A Q5): Afib: Stopping warfarin one week prior to surgery to normalize coagulation poses little risk of stroke’ davidson’
expl: AF on warfarin before lumpectomy: stop warfarin ahead of time (3–5 days to 1 week in the older key), bridge with heparin if needed, restart a few days after surgery.

why.D: Still anticoagulated.

stem: A child was scheduled for elective inguinal hernia repair, before surgery he got severe bilateral wheeze what to do in this situation?

opts.t: Local anesthesia and avoid excessive airway manipulation

expl: Severe bilateral wheeze before an elective operation → postpone and treat; elective surgery should not be done during an acute attack.

why.B: Elective surgery can wait; don't proceed in active bronchospasm.
why.C: Proceeding the same day is unsafe.
why.D: Doesn't treat acute bronchospasm.

stem: A 12 years old child assigned for elective inguinal hernia repair, preoperatively he presented with bilateral severe chest wheezing, what is your next action?

opts.t: Local anesthesia and avoid excessive airway manipulation

expl: The source keyed B and marked it "not sure". In a 436 duplicate of the same scenario the key is A (postpone). For an elective case with severe wheeze, postponing is the safer, standard answer.

why.A: Spinal block + steroids is not standard for a 12-year-old in active bronchospasm.
why.B: Source key ("not sure") — local anesthesia avoids airway manipulation, but elective surgery can be postponed.
why.C: Proceeding the same day is unsafe.
why.D: Doesn't treat the acute attack.

stem: A 40 Year-old obese male was booked for a day surgery, anesthetic review preopertively assesed him as (low to intermediate risk),which of the following is the most likely cause?
expl: BMI 30–40 = mild systemic disease (ASA II) → low-to-intermediate risk; that is why he was rated so. Age 40 isn't a risk factor by itself.

why.D: Age 40 is not a significant risk factor.

stem: 45 years old came for elective breast reduction surgery, doctor to operate after that you received a complaint from the patient stating that doctor is refusing to operate on her for no reason. You check her labs and it shows as follow: Fasting blood glucose 120 mg/dl HB 12 HBA1c 14 What are you going to tell the patient?

opts.t: You agree with her complaint there's no reason for cancelling the surgery
You agree with doctor decision because she's high risk
You agree with patient complain because it's cosmetic surgery
You agree with doctor decision cause she has low Hb level

srcNote: (Pre-operative assessment) The patient has unstable diabetes. ASA 3
expl: HbA1c 14 = very poorly controlled diabetes (ASA 3). For an elective cosmetic operation, the risk of infection and metabolic complications is high → optimize first. The surgeon is right.

why.C: Cosmetic surgery is exactly the kind that should wait.
why.D: Hb 12 is acceptable.

stem: Which one of the following should be included in the informed consent?
srcNote: (Patient safety) Informed consent: Details & accuracy of the dx, the goal and details of the planned procedure, complications, prognosis, other tx options, advantages and possibility of success, name of responsible surgeon, at any time, the patient can change his or her mind.
expl: Informed consent includes the diagnosis, the planned procedure, complications, prognosis, other options, and the name of the responsible surgeon.

why.D: Not part of consent.

stem: “Sign in” involves which of the following?
srcNote: (Patient safety) Sign in: Confirmation of patient identity Site and nature of procedure Obtaining consent Marking the site of procedure
expl: Sign in = confirm patient identity, site, procedure, consent, site marking (before induction). Counting gauzes = sign out.

why.D: Part of sign out.

stem: A 60 y/o man was admitted with marked weight loss due to carcinoma of the lower esophagus. Which of the following is the appropriate method to improve his nutritional status before surgery?
expl: Source key: central parenteral nutrition. Reasoning used by the key: an obstructing lower esophageal cancer limits enteral access, and a gastrostomy would damage the stomach needed as the esophageal conduit. (Another version of this question keyed gastrostomy because the gut is usable.)

why.A: Peripheral PN cannot deliver enough calories for marked weight loss.
why.C: Keyed in the 429 version; the stomach is usually preserved for reconstruction.
why.D: A tube may not pass an obstructing tumor.

stem: A 30 year old patient admitted through emergency department with diagnosis of acute appendicitis. He was booked for an emergent appendectomy under general anesthesia. The patient is asthmatic which is well controlled with medications. According to American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status of this patient will be which of the following?
expl: Well-controlled asthma = mild systemic disease (ASA 2), and the operation is an emergency → add "E": ASA 2E.

why.A: He has a systemic disease, so not ASA 1.
why.D: Missing the E and over-grades him.

stem: A 3 months old baby has to undergo circumcision under general anesthesia. The baby is on infant formula milk. You will advise the mother to keep the baby fasting for how many hours before surgery? *
expl: Infant formula = 6 hours fasting (breast milk 4 h, clear fluids 1–2 h).

why.D: Longer than needed.

stem: A 65 y\o man, presented to outpatient clinic complaining of epigastric pain and early satiety for 3 months. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed antral gastric mass. Confirmed by biopsy and histopathology to be adenocarcinoma. Patient was consented for surgery.Which of the following low blood level is suggestive of nutritional deficiency?
expl: Serum albumin is the classic marker of nutritional status/protein deficiency before surgery (low albumin = more complications).

why.C: Transferrin also falls but albumin is the standard answer.
why.D: Iron reflects iron stores, not overall nutrition.

stem: A 27 y/o lady reported to the ER with severe abdominal pain . The gynecologist diagnosed her to be… ruptured ectopic pregnancy and want to operate her as an emergency case. The patient … a known diabetic. Her preoperative blood sugar level is 13 mmol/l.Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Ask for ECG, chest X-ray and electrolytes estimation before surgery.
Ask for nephrology and cardiology consultation before surgery.

expl: Ruptured ectopic = life-threatening haemorrhage. Glucose 13 mmol/L is not a reason to delay; operate now and manage glucose peri-operatively.

why.D: Correct.

stem: 60 y o man was admitted with marked weight loss due to carcinoma of the lower esophagus. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to improve his nutritional status?

opts.t: Gastrostomy feeding (this is for long TERM)

srcNote: (Nutrition in surgical patients) Patient can use his GI system, but it was answered as TPN. Source note (428 Q6): Answer: C, Patient still can use his GI.
expl: Source key (428/429): gastrostomy, because "the patient can still use his GI tract" — enteral feeding beats parenteral when the gut works. Another version keyed central PN.

why.D: Tube may not pass an obstructing tumor.
